what's your name Charles E Love what's the E for Edward that's a part of my father name Charles E Love
and what's your name oh Bill Russell's here Ralph Collins Ralph say something so the secretary I know you thank you for the introduction William Russell what's your
name saying your own word Ralph Collins and my name is Dick Allen okay we got it set up we were talking about Emmett Hardy a minute ago and you said you knew him
huh did you have a play with him did he sit in with you no I never played with him but even I was working at different places I used to meet him and talk sometime only on his way home
went over the ferry together and I used to see him did he have any did he have any special finger in
or anything I was wondering yeah he used artificial fingers sometimes artificially called it

mm-hmm what he was he very fast and fingering on yes he was very fast he's a nice trumpet player what kind of a tone did he have very good tone did you say it was sweet or ratty or well it was on the sweet side I see can you put on that record of jasmine blues Bill for him who does this sound like dear Mm-hm.
You sound like mud.
Sound like mud there now. Mud carry.
Mud carry.
Mud carry. Mud carry. Mud carry. Mud carry. Did the trumpet sound like mud all the way through or just at times? Mud sounds like mud to me. Mud carry. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. So back to Hardy, do you remember who he worked with over there, across the river?

Well, he worked with different fellows. He worked on Bourbon Street sometimes, and different places, spots around. During the time I was working on Ivoryville Street for the E-light, because I used to meet him, going to wake, and sometimes we'd go over together on the boat in the morning. He used to wake all around in Vichy Corral.
What about Jelly Roll Morton? You said you knew him too, huh?

Jelly Roll? Uh-huh. I don't know him this piano school. He used to be here a while back on Bayeson Street. And he left here. He went around Monroe, went home, and from there he'd come back here again. He played piano all over around Vichy Corral, mostly on Basin Street, mostly. Who would he be working for? And in 1917, he went back home again in 1917, he came to Chicago. And he'd be around at 35th and State at the E-light Cabaret. Used to visit there, you know. Every night when the music, they had a band that they'd play a couple of numbers, they'd call on him and he'd play piano, you know, sometimes. They'd go out to the cottage, go, different nightclubs, you know. On the south side, playing number too, you know. Then he had work he used to do of his own. Around there, I don't know what place.
Was that his name at that time, Charlie?
His name was Morton.
Was he known as?

Known as Jelly Roll. Used to call him that. He picked up that name around when Clance William was down there, you see. He wrote a piece about, ain't gonna give nobody none of my Jelly Roll, you see. And he used to play it so well, you know, with Clance. And he just called him Jelly Roll Morton.
Did he sing at all, Charlie?
I never did know that boy's real name, his first name. They called him Jelly Roll Morton, that's all I know about him. He's a good ragtime piano player.
He didn't do any singing, did he?
Oh yeah, he used to sing some numbers, but he mostly played well. I see.
Where was he from? Monroe.
Monroe, Louisiana.
And where did he work on Basin Street? Do you remember what house it?

I think he worked at Lula White's for a while. Then he worked at some other house, I don't know what the name of it. These fellas used to change around, you know, and playing like that. He used to play around 25 sometimes, you know, just in the daytime like that. And he'd go out, go around there and play a few numbers.
Just a second. Talking about Jelly Roll, Basin Street and Monroe, and where else did you know him?

In Shreveport. He'd come around Shreveport. You know, musicians at that time used to travel around different places to play, and if he'd strike a good job, why, he'd stay there for a while. When the job run out, well of course he'd always take a trip home somewhere and then find another place. In 1917, I remember, he was in Chicago.
When did you know him in Shreveport? About what year?
Let me see about what time. I couldn't say exactly, but I know it was...
I see. Well, I'll put it this way. Was it before the big storm or after? Would that help you?
Yes. Yeah, it was the storm. That was 1915.
Yeah, the storm was in 1915.
One of them there, two storms there. I think this must be around, I say about 19... 1914 or 15, somewhere along there.
It was about the time of the storm then, huh? Approximately, roughly. Well, let me see. What was the first band to leave here and go into the North? Into the North? That you remember.
Eddie Vance and Jimmy Paul. Let me see what band they call that.
We can figure it out. Who else was in the band?

I'll tell you. Eddie Vance and Trombone and Jimmy Paul. His right name is Jimmy Spriggs, but they called him Jimmy Paul. I don't know for what reason. Eddie Vance and Jimmy Paul, Big Eye Louie and Freddie Kepard. Now the other two guitar men, I can't think of who it was. Maybe you can pick that up from some other music. Did you know the bass player? The bass player? I think it was Bro. Bro, huh? I don't know which bro. They got two of them bros, you know.
You don't know which bro? There was two bros, huh? I think so.
This fellow was around here, I think. He's young. McNeil, bro. Huh?
McNeil, bro. He's here and Wellman, bro, is the old one. That's the one.
It must have been him. The old bro. Because he's right in age with Pauli and Vincent.
What was Pauli playing in that time?
Jimmy Pauli? Violin. He was a fine violin player.
Did he ever play any other instruments?

He played melliforne in the brass band, in the Pacific Brass Band. And they tell me after he left here, he learned how to play saxophone. When he come back to Chicago, he died in Chicago. He stayed there, you know, him and Vincent Bo.
Well I've seen a picture of him playing saxophone.
And Big Eye Louie come back and Kepard stayed there too in Chicago. Kepard never did come back. Died there. Died there.
Yeah, I think he used to play saxophone with Dewey. Who was that? In a picture.
Of Palau. Palau. Yeah, he learned saxophone. I don't know what saxophone he played, but to tell me he was good at it. I know he was a first class violin player and a mellophone player.
Well when did Eddie Vincent leave?
Oh, I was a real young dude then. That was way back.
Would it be 1900 or would it be 1910 or 1920 or what?

No, I don't think it was that far back. That's it. Dewey used to wait on Basin Street, Emmanuel Perez. That's when I was very small. Yeah, that must bring back. Let's see, wait, I got to get that thing straight. I think Tom could tell you better than I could about that. Tom Alba? Yeah. Because I had learned how to play cornet, you know, and Tom was playing the violin. And Eddie Vincent was practicing every day with us. And then all at once he picked up and he left there with Jimmy Fallon and then we went north. Well, he learned a lot when he was gone, you know. Went all over the Pantages time, I think they call it. All around and they come back, you see. Stomped in Chicago. Well, I was gone. I had been there and left. That was about around, well, I don't want to say because I don't know exactly. But it must have been 19, it was 1917. Because I remember Freddie Kepard come in and him and I played together, you know, on a show one night. We were giving a term for a sick musician in the roadhouse. We played together and I didn't get to see Louie or none of them. I flew around and I left Chicago and come back to Shreveport. Later after that, got Louie come in. Freddie stayed. And that left Louie, yeah, he got him another job around here, working around, you know, a different band. And when I left Shreveport, I come back to New Orleans. And Andrew Kimball was playing the cornet at the Lyric Theater with John Robichaud. And John told me Kimball was going to leave, you know. And said, the theater's closed now. I said, Kimball gonna leave. And I would have the job. And said, you about the fella for this job. You been playing shows. I said, well, I'd like to get you to play with me in the theater when it opens. I said, well, when it's gonna open? And he said, well, I don't know exactly, but three or four weeks after the repair up and everything, I said, I got Big Eye Louie gonna play clarinet with me and you and him oughta work good together. So I had taken the job and kept playing around at ELITE Cabaret, they call it. And they closed. And when they closed, they had another place open up there on Franklin, right over from 25, called it Lawler's Cabaret. Well, I got a job done. I worked right along. Up until the theater opened, I notified the fellow that I couldn't work any long because I promised John Robichaud I was going to work with him in the theater. So he wanted me to stay. He liked the way I played and everything. He wanted me to stay. Lee Collins had left here and went to Memphis. When he went to Memphis, he thought about Lee. He said, I can get you a good corner. He said, no, I want you. I said, how about Lee Collins? He says, oh yeah, that's right. Why could I reach Lee? I said, he's in Memphis. So somebody told him to address me. He wired Lee, you know. I gave him a two weeks notice, you know. Man, you're so glad to get Lee, you see. You know Lee could play that kind of music, you know. So he sent for Lee. And I had two weeks coming. He didn't pay no attention to that. He said, well, you can leave Wednesday coming. He said, he doesn't come back now, you know. I heard Lee was in town, you know. So to let him go to work too, I just told him I wasn't coming back no more. I went home and Lee took the job. He stayed there for a while. Then Lee went away. And Kid Punch took the job. Him and George, your boy, and they had a swinging little old band around there, you know. That stuff like to play around there, you know. And he took the job. Well, I got a job in other places then, you know. Left there. I had left and Lee took the job and then Poins taken. Let me see what I done. Then I had a job with Big Eye and Louis before the theater opened up, you know. And the next following week, me and Louis went to work together. No, we went together before when I went back. Piku was on that job. He was playing the alto strikes and playing there. Where did you work with them? So the union, the union, they got up a union and Piku didn't want to get in there, you see. And so they sent and got Louis anyway. Then me and Louis was working together. We had a girl playing piano. She was a very good musician. They called me. I told them about her, you know, and they placed her in the place of Miss Margaret. She's a great piano player too.
Miss Margaret?

Miss Margaret. Kimber's wife. They come back, you know. They went to Hot Spring. Lucius Wilson wanted me to come there to play, you see. And I knew Kimber was the man for him. So I told Kimber. And his wife was playing all the time in May and Neely. Before May and Neely. That's the way it was at the theater. And her and Kimber had taken this job and went to work for Lucius J. Wilson. I don't know for what reason. Well, he didn't work long. About two or three months. The job blew up or something. And he come back to Shreveport where I had been playing around there. At the Star Theater. I believe he went in there. They call it. Across the street. They call it. What the theater in there. Hippodrome. Called the Hippodrome Theater. Right across the street from the Star Theater. I used to work at the Star. In Shreveport? In Shreveport. In Shreveport. So Kimber and his wife went to work there. And I was working with John Rubishow in the place where he had just left, you see. I don't know what would come of him after that. He went on out in Hot Springs somewhere again. I think he died. He come back there before he died. I don't know whether his wife lived or not. She must be dead too. They were very old people, you know.

When was the first time you ever met Big Guy? Do you remember? Me? Oh, when I was nothing but a kid. He used to come up to the town where I was in Plackman, Plackman, Louisiana. Used to come up there with Manny Perez, you know. He was a very young fellow himself at that time. And when they were going to play a dance there at the Oddfellas Hall, you know, I always kept with musicians along that time. They had a little pool hall right on there.

They were on the corner by the station. And they had a rooming house there, you know. The band used to get room there. And everybody would be out walking around the town. Louie would be in the room there blowing that clarinet. And I was crazy about the clarinet, you know, but I couldn't play it. I'd listen at him like that. And when he'd come out, you know, he'd say, hello there. I'd say, hello there, fella. He'd have a little love here. He'd say, yeah, come on in. I'd go in and sit down. He'd practice there all day. Go get his dinner and come back and just stay on that clarinet. All the pieces he had to play that night, he'd run over, you know. And he'd get tired playing. He was a particular fella that cleaned his clarinet up nice. Blow a cup in the old seats, all right, put it in the case, you see. Always a dick, the fella, nice and clean, always wore nice clothes. And he'd come out to catch the air, you know, go around and drink. He'd like to drink good whiskey. Go around and get him a cup of whiskey. And that night, man, he couldn't hear nothing but that clarinet. You know, man, it was a loud, bright cornet player. Loud! And Louie was right there with him, you know. He could do anything, man, he could do on the cornet, you know. He'd answer them with that clarinet. And I'd stay there until it's all over before I'd go home. Sometimes they didn't allow me. I was late at night. My paus knew where I'm at, you know. He'd come get me. I'd sit right behind Louie and listen at him, you see. Emmanuel and I thought they were great musicians, you know.
You know if Louie, did he read much or did he play mostly by ear in those days?

Well at that time they had, well, easy music, it wasn't hard to play. And they played mostly by note because Emmanuel was a good reader. And to keep up, that's why Louie played so hard and practiced. He practiced from the music then? Yeah, practiced from the music. He had his music, sheet music, you know, and he'd play it. Didn't suit him. He'd shake his head, take a rest, come back. Again, come back to it. When he'd get that tune finished, put that one up and get another one, you know, run over the whole repertoire. And that night, man, he'd have it down. And he'd come down there when he'd come back home, you know. Just one night, play the dance, come back down there, and if you happen, come down too and go by and Romy would be doing that same thing, practicing. He practiced regularly. It made him perfect. He was one of the sweetest clarinet players. They had around there. At that time he was playing C, C melody. And they didn't have any violin player in the band. So Louie played a violin part with that C clarinet. Man, this is sweet.
Did you ever play clarinet? Huh?

Did you ever play clarinet? No, I never did, but I loved it. Did you ever try? Well I blowed a few notes on it. It was complicated, you know, and I was so crazy about that cornet, I didn't have time to learn, you know. And I put all my efforts on the trumpet. What other instruments have you ever played? I played the drums. I played the drums. I played that before I played the trumpet, you see. My father was a cornet player, you know. And he didn't allow nobody to touch his instruments. We had a room full of instruments there, you know. When he'd go to work then I'd try them all. I'd try all the instruments, you know. And I'd see him take to the cornet, you know. And I'd, Mom would run me out the house with a broom or anything. I'd go out, we had an old bogey house in the backyard. Go out there and shut the door, you know, and blow all day. Well she wouldn't bother me, you know. But she didn't want me to play it, cornet. She wanted me to be a violin player. She said I was too delicate, I might not make it, you know. Injured myself. So she bought me a violin. I didn't like that thing. I couldn't do nothing with that. That was complicated, you know. I didn't take no lessons or nothing with it. I tried to fake with it. After a while I picked up a little bit. But I used to watch my dad all the time, how he'd play, you know. And I loved that. Things I'd yell him make on the horn, I couldn't, didn't know nothing about music. And the time he'd go to work, I'd steal one of them horns and they had a brass band, you see. But I wouldn't fool with his and I'd take one of them other ones. I didn't know whether it was an E flat or B flat and go back in that stable. Me and that horn. And I used to hear him say he didn't like to play E flat. He used to come down, yeah, you know, playing the Pickwick band sometimes when they needed an E flat player. They didn't have many of them then. Frank Robinson, he was in Baden Rouge, David Bowhill and my father. He played both, B flat and E flat, but he didn't like brass bands. See, he didn't like playing no E flat. So finally he gave that thing away. I used to play a B flat. That's getting one off the floor there somewhere. We had a whole room full of instruments. And I liked the lighting that thing. I went, my pa took me to a circus one day. And I don't know what cornet player that was. It was a big fat fella, you know, he was standing up directing. I believe he was playing his left hand directing with a stick. And man, that sounds good to me. He used to crack cornet player. And I said, that's my instrument. I went right on home and grabbed it. Papa went to work. He used to make handmade singles on the bial, cypress singles. When he'd get to work. And then I'd get to work on one of them B flat cornets. And I'd come as to make noise with it, you know. My pa caught me several times. I'd go, put that horn down. Get that violin. You want to play? Put that thing down. You ain't, you never learn no cornet like that, you know. I didn't want him to tell me that, you know. A fella tell me I couldn't do something. I'd show him. I'd do it anyhow, you know. So he went to work. I'd bring his dinner and things sometime, come home, you know. He'd practice all the time too, in the evening and in the morning before he'd go to work. He'd come in that evening. My mother named Kate said, Kate, fix me something good. Now I'm going to practice a little while. They'd go in that room where all them instruments had to get that B flat cornet, you know. Something the band had together. They used to make all them music. They didn't buy no music. They'd make up their own music. So he'd play his cornet. It sounds so good, you know. I'd fool around there, he'd come out and get him a drink of coffee or something like that. Steal him out in my old B flat and go out in the buggy house. He'd be playing away, you know. And I'd be finding a note to fix what that he was doing, you know. One day he heard when he stopped. When he stopped, I used to stop too, you know. Man, it got good to him, you know. He went to playing again, you know. And I'd come into making some little notes with him, you know, and he heard it. Say, boy, what's that you? Ain't you got a horn out there? I said, come here. I had a horn behind him, you know. He said, I know that you're out there. I said, what's that you was making on that? It sounds good to him, you see. So he played a little piece and said, see if you can do that again. Now I could make good noise. And he'd start to play it and I'd do it with him, you know. Sometimes I'd make a bad one, you know. He wouldn't say nothing. He'd look at me and say, well, you just got something in that head anyhow. And I wanted to go to Tuskegee College, you see. I used to save all my nickels, dimes and everything. I wanted to go to school.
What were you going to study? Any particular?

At first I wanted to study bricklayers trade. My uncle used to come home, you know, and they'd have a time there, you know. It looked like he had more money than anybody else. He'd just take it out, you know, and tell him get something to drink what you like. They'd have whiskey drinking and wine drinking take place there, you know. And my uncle would have all that and wanted this. Didn't know what to do with it. Yeah, boy. Give me a dollar or anything. And all the kids. So I wanted to be a bricklayer like him so I could have a pocket full of money, you know. And Papa told me, he said, you too delicate. I can't let you go. I said, you'll have to die before we can get to you if you take sick or something like that. And they wouldn't let me. You know, I was easy. And it's a good thing I listen to my people too. I was an easy kid. They said, you just can't go. He said, if you stay home. I had done made plenty of money to go to start the first year, you see. Second year, I was going to work on my trade. I paid for my school and everything. Well, I had that on my mind. So, he wouldn't let me go. Papa said, if you don't go, I'll let you go down to Algiers and stay with your cousin. You might get a chance to go to night school at the street. He said, it won't cost so much money. You can so much a day at school and eat with your cousin over in Algiers and stay there. He said, but a boarding school like that, he said, after you spent all your money, then you make me spend all of mine. He said, you better go down there with your cousin, then you might find what you want to do. So, I come down and he was just fixing to build that Navy out there. And, you know, dug out and everything is pouring. Going to pour concrete, you see. Going to make all them buildings of concrete. So, I went out there. I was small, so small to, I had big fellas there. Like, in here, handing them shovels, you see. And they had a little run about 12 inches wide, about that high from the ground. Keep from rolling that cement on the mud, you see. They lift that board that high. So, I went out there looking for work, you know. I seen them big fellas, little ones too, you know. Rolling that stuff out. Watched them, you know. Fella come around and said, boy, the boss, you know. Boy, what do you want around there? I said. I come around and see if I could get a job. He said, we ain't hiring babies around here. We hiring men. And what were you about? Huh?
About how old you?
I don't know. I must have been about 15 or 16 years old at that time. So, my man said, you can't get no work. Yeah, I left. That made me feel bad. I left. That made me feel bad.
The last interview we had a month ago, you were telling about the trombone players like Eddie Benson over in Algiers. Could you tell us some more about him when you first met him?
When I first met him, I was working at the Navy Yard and I used to hear them fellas practicing over there.

segments.title: Recording setup, names and date
segments.summary: Sound check and introductions; interview dated January 16, 1960, with Charles E. Love, Bill Russell and Dick Allen.

segments.title: Emmett Hardy: his playing, fingers and tone, where he worked
segments.summary: Love knew Hardy from meeting on the ferry but never played with him; Hardy was fast, sweet-toned and used artificial fingers. A record is played and discussed, then Hardy's jobs across the river.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton in New Orleans and Chicago, and how he got his name
segments.summary: Love recalls Morton playing piano on Basin Street, at Lula White's, and in Chicago in 1917; the Jelly Roll name came from a piece played with Clarence Williams.

segments.title: Dating Morton's visits to Shreveport
segments.summary: Morton travelled to Shreveport; Love dates it around the 1915 storm, about 1914-15.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the Northern migration
segments.title: First New Orleans band to go north: Vincent, Palao, Big Eye Louis, Keppard
segments.summary: Love names the members of the first band to leave for the North, their instruments, who stayed in Chicago and who came back, and tries to date Vincent's departure.

segments.title: Love's own jobs: Lyric Theater, Robichaux, Lee Collins and Kid Punch
segments.summary: In one long account Love covers 1917 Chicago, returning to New Orleans, the Lyric Theater job with Robichaux, Cabaret work, replacement by Lee Collins, and working with Big Eye Louis.

segments.title: Miss Margaret and Kimball: Hot Springs and Shreveport theaters
segments.summary: Love describes Kimball's wife the pianist, their job in Hot Springs and return to the Hippodrome in Shreveport, while Love worked at the Star.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Louis and Love's boyhood
segments.title: Meeting Big Eye Louis as a boy in Plaquemine
segments.summary: Love first met Louis when he came with Manuel Perez's band to play a dance; he describes Louis practicing clarinet all day.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Louis and Love's boyhood
segments.title: Big Eye Louis reading music and practicing
segments.summary: The band played mostly by note, Louis practiced from sheet music, played C-melody clarinet and covered the violin part.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Louis and Love's boyhood
segments.title: Love's own instruments and learning cornet from his father
segments.summary: Love never played clarinet; he began on drums, secretly practiced his cornet-playing father's instruments, resisted his mother's wish for violin, and got his father's help.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Louis and Love's boyhood
segments.title: Wanting Tuskegee and the bricklayer trade; refused work at the Navy yard
segments.summary: Love wanted to go to school and learn bricklaying, his father refused, and he was turned away from a construction job in Algiers at about 15 or 16.

segments.title: Trombonist Eddie Benson of Algiers
segments.summary: Russell asks about Eddie Benson; Love says he first heard him practicing while working at the Navy Yard.

segments.title: Playback of a solo
segments.summary: A brief question about where a solo on a playback was first heard.
